The writer effectively uses sensory details to create a tangible and believable atmosphere. The story engages the sense of sight (the dense fog hiding the opposite shore, the dew-covered spiderweb, the black water, the overly bright phone screen in the grey light), sound (the deep, even hum of the idling engine, footsteps on gravel, the soft groaning of the ferry as it departs, the buzzing of the phone against the metal surface), and touch (the cold, dripping wet cable that the boy touches, the worn monthly pass with a bent corner, the vibration of the phone against Ilse's hip). These specific details ground the reader in the chilly, quiet November morning on the river.
